title: Industrial Chemistry
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 300L industrial chemistry curriculum: major industrial processes (Haber, Contact, Solvay, petroleum refining and petrochemicals), metal extraction, cement and glass manufacture, soap/detergent and fertiliser production, industrial catalysis, unit operations, water treatment, and industrial pollution/corrosion control.

questions.question: The Haber process for industrial ammonia synthesis combines nitrogen and hydrogen gases under which typical operating conditions?
options: Low pressure, low temperature, no catalyst
High pressure (~200 atm), moderate temperature (~450 degC), iron catalyst
Atmospheric pressure, very high temperature (~1000 degC), platinum catalyst
Vacuum conditions with a copper catalyst
questions.correct_answer: High pressure (~200 atm), moderate temperature (~450 degC), iron catalyst
questions.explanation: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 is exothermic and proceeds with a decrease in gas moles, so high pressure and a compromise (moderate) temperature with an iron catalyst (promoted with K2O/Al2O3) are used industrially to balance yield and rate.

questions.question: In the Haber process, increasing the operating pressure favours a higher equilibrium yield of ammonia mainly because:
options: The forward reaction produces fewer moles of gas, so Le Chatelier's principle favours the forward direction under higher pressure
Ammonia is a liquid at high pressure
Higher pressure destroys the catalyst
Pressure has no effect on gas-phase equilibria
questions.correct_answer: The forward reaction produces fewer moles of gas, so Le Chatelier's principle favours the forward direction under higher pressure
questions.explanation: Since 4 moles of gaseous reactants form 2 moles of product, increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium toward the side with fewer gas moles, i.e. toward ammonia.

questions.question: The Contact process for industrial sulfuric acid production involves the catalytic oxidation of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide using which catalyst?
options: Finely divided iron
Vanadium(V) oxide (V2O5)
Nickel
Platinum only, with no alternative catalyst ever used
questions.correct_answer: Vanadium(V) oxide (V2O5)
questions.explanation: V2O5 is the standard industrial catalyst for 2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3, chosen for its lower cost and resistance to catalyst poisoning compared with platinum.

questions.question: In the Contact process, SO3 is not absorbed directly into water to form H2SO4 industrially because this would:
options: Produce a dense, corrosive acid mist that is difficult to condense and control
Immediately decompose SO3 into SO2
Produce hydrogen gas as a hazardous by-product
Reduce the reaction rate to zero
questions.correct_answer: Produce a dense, corrosive acid mist that is difficult to condense and control
questions.explanation: Direct absorption of SO3 in water is highly exothermic and forms a fine, hard-to-condense acid mist; industrially SO3 is instead absorbed in concentrated H2SO4 to form oleum, which is then diluted.

questions.question: The Solvay process is used industrially to manufacture which compound?
options: Sodium carbonate (Na2CO3)
Sodium chloride (NaCl)
Sodium hydroxide (NaOH)
Sodium sulfate (Na2SO4)
questions.correct_answer: Sodium carbonate (Na2CO3)
questions.explanation: The Solvay process converts brine and limestone (via ammonia and CO2) into sodium carbonate (soda ash), a key industrial alkali.

questions.question: In the Solvay process, sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) precipitates when carbon dioxide and ammonia are passed into brine because:
options: NaHCO3 is more soluble than NaCl in the ammoniated brine
NaHCO3 has relatively low solubility in the cold, ammoniated, CO2-saturated brine and crystallises out
Ammonia reacts directly with NaCl to form NaHCO3 gas
The reaction produces only gaseous products
questions.correct_answer: NaHCO3 has relatively low solubility in the cold, ammoniated, CO2-saturated brine and crystallises out
questions.explanation: NaHCO3 is the least soluble species present under these conditions, so it selectively crystallises and is filtered off, then calcined to give Na2CO3.

questions.question: Fractional distillation of crude petroleum separates its components mainly on the basis of differences in:
options: Colour
Boiling point
Density alone
Electrical conductivity
questions.correct_answer: Boiling point
questions.explanation: Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons with different boiling points; fractional distillation exploits these differences to separate fractions such as gasoline, kerosene, diesel, and residue.

questions.question: Catalytic cracking of heavy petroleum fractions is carried out primarily to:
options: Increase the average molecular weight of the hydrocarbons
Break large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more commercially valuable ones such as petrol
Remove sulfur compounds only
Convert alkanes into alcohols
questions.correct_answer: Break large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more commercially valuable ones such as petrol
questions.explanation: Cracking converts high-boiling, low-demand heavy fractions into lighter, more valuable products like petrol and petrochemical feedstocks (alkenes), typically using a zeolite catalyst.

questions.question: Octane number is a measure used to describe:
options: The sulfur content of a fuel
The resistance of a petrol/gasoline fuel to knocking (premature ignition) in a spark-ignition engine
The boiling point of diesel fuel
The viscosity of lubricating oil
questions.correct_answer: The resistance of a petrol/gasoline fuel to knocking (premature ignition) in a spark-ignition engine
questions.explanation: Octane number rates a fuel's anti-knock performance relative to reference mixtures of iso-octane and heptane; higher octane numbers indicate greater resistance to knocking.

questions.question: Petrochemicals such as ethylene and propylene, used as feedstocks for plastics manufacture, are primarily obtained industrially by:
options: Steam cracking of naphtha or natural gas liquids
Direct distillation of crude petroleum without further processing
Fermentation of sugars
Electrolysis of brine
questions.correct_answer: Steam cracking of naphtha or natural gas liquids
questions.explanation: Steam cracking thermally breaks saturated hydrocarbon feedstocks into smaller alkenes (ethylene, propylene) that serve as building blocks for polymers and other petrochemicals.

questions.question: In the industrial extraction of iron in the blast furnace, coke serves mainly as:
options: A drying agent
Both a fuel and a reducing agent, converting iron oxide to iron via carbon monoxide
An oxidising agent
A catalyst that is not consumed
questions.correct_answer: Both a fuel and a reducing agent, converting iron oxide to iron via carbon monoxide
questions.explanation: Coke burns to generate heat and CO, and CO reduces iron oxides (Fe2O3, Fe3O4) to molten iron in the blast furnace: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2.

questions.question: Limestone is added to the blast furnace during iron extraction mainly to:
options: Increase the melting point of iron
React with silica (sand) impurities to form slag, which is removed separately from the molten iron
Serve as the primary fuel
Act as the reducing agent
questions.correct_answer: React with silica (sand) impurities to form slag, which is removed separately from the molten iron
questions.explanation: Limestone decomposes to CaO, which reacts with acidic impurities like SiO2 to form calcium silicate (slag), a less dense liquid that floats above and is separated from molten iron.

questions.question: Industrial extraction of aluminium from purified alumina (Al2O3) by the Hall-Heroult process requires electrolysis because:
options: Aluminium is too reactive to be reduced by carbon at achievable furnace temperatures, so electrolytic reduction is used instead
Alumina is a liquid at room temperature
Aluminium oxide conducts electricity in the solid state
Carbon reduction produces pure aluminium directly at low temperature
questions.correct_answer: Aluminium is too reactive to be reduced by carbon at achievable furnace temperatures, so electrolytic reduction is used instead
questions.explanation: Aluminium's strong affinity for oxygen makes carbon reduction thermodynamically impractical at normal furnace temperatures, so molten alumina dissolved in cryolite is electrolysed instead.

questions.question: Cryolite (Na3AlF6) is added to alumina in the Hall-Heroult process primarily to:
options: Act as the electrolyte and lower the melting point of alumina, reducing energy costs
Serve as the anode material
Prevent any current from flowing
Oxidise the aluminium produced
questions.correct_answer: Act as the electrolyte and lower the melting point of alumina, reducing energy costs
questions.explanation: Pure alumina melts above 2000 degC; dissolving it in molten cryolite lowers the melting point to around 950-980 degC, making electrolysis economically feasible.

questions.question: The main raw materials for the manufacture of ordinary Portland cement are:
options: Limestone and clay
Sodium chloride and sulfuric acid
Bauxite and cryolite
Sulfur and coke
questions.correct_answer: Limestone and clay
questions.explanation: Cement is made by heating a mixture of limestone (calcium carbonate) and clay (aluminosilicates) in a rotary kiln to form clinker, which is then ground with gypsum.

questions.question: Gypsum is added to cement clinker during grinding mainly to:
options: Control (retard) the setting time of the cement
Increase the colour intensity of the cement
Act as the primary binding compound
Remove water from the clinker
questions.correct_answer: Control (retard) the setting time of the cement
questions.explanation: Gypsum regulates the hydration rate of tricalcium aluminate, preventing flash setting and allowing workable setting times for construction use.

questions.question: Ordinary soda-lime glass is manufactured mainly by melting together silica (sand), sodium carbonate, and:
options: Calcium carbonate (limestone)
Sodium chloride
Sulfuric acid
Aluminium metal
questions.correct_answer: Calcium carbonate (limestone)
questions.explanation: Soda-lime glass is formed by fusing silica sand with soda ash (Na2CO3, lowers the melting point) and limestone (CaCO3, improves chemical durability).

questions.question: Saponification, the chemical reaction underlying soap manufacture, is best described as the:
options: Oxidation of fatty acids to carbon dioxide
Alkaline hydrolysis of fats/oils (triglycerides) to give glycerol and fatty acid salts (soap)
Esterification of glycerol with fatty acids
Chlorination of fatty acids
questions.correct_answer: Alkaline hydrolysis of fats/oils (triglycerides) to give glycerol and fatty acid salts (soap)
questions.explanation: Triglycerides are hydrolysed by a strong base (e.g. NaOH) into glycerol and the sodium salts of long-chain fatty acids, which are soaps.

questions.question: Synthetic detergents, unlike ordinary soaps, remain effective in hard water mainly because:
options: They form insoluble scum/precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions, just like soap
Their sulfonate or sulfate head groups form soluble salts with calcium and magnesium ions rather than insoluble precipitates
They contain no hydrophobic tail
They react chemically with hard water to remove it
questions.correct_answer: Their sulfonate or sulfate head groups form soluble salts with calcium and magnesium ions rather than insoluble precipitates
questions.explanation: Unlike carboxylate soaps, which precipitate as insoluble calcium/magnesium salts (scum) in hard water, sulfonate/sulfate-based detergents form soluble Ca2+/Mg2+ salts, retaining cleaning action.

questions.question: The industrial synthesis of nitric acid (Ostwald process) begins with the catalytic oxidation of ammonia over a platinum-rhodium catalyst to give:
options: Nitrogen dioxide directly
Nitric oxide (NO)
Ammonium nitrate
Nitrous oxide only
questions.correct_answer: Nitric oxide (NO)
questions.explanation: 4NH3 + 5O2 -> 4NO + 6H2O over a Pt-Rh gauze catalyst is the first step; NO is then further oxidised to NO2 and absorbed in water to form HNO3.

questions.question: Superphosphate fertiliser is produced industrially by treating phosphate rock with:
options: Sulfuric acid (or phosphoric acid for triple superphosphate)
Sodium hydroxide
Ammonia gas only
Chlorine gas
questions.correct_answer: Sulfuric acid (or phosphoric acid for triple superphosphate)
questions.explanation: Treating insoluble calcium phosphate rock with sulfuric acid converts it to soluble calcium dihydrogen phosphate (superphosphate); using phosphoric acid instead gives the more concentrated triple superphosphate.

questions.question: Urea, a widely used nitrogenous fertiliser, is industrially synthesised from:
options: Ammonia and carbon dioxide under heat and pressure
Nitric acid and calcium carbonate
Sulfuric acid and ammonia only
Sodium nitrate and potassium chloride
questions.correct_answer: Ammonia and carbon dioxide under heat and pressure
questions.explanation: The industrial urea process reacts ammonia with carbon dioxide to form ammonium carbamate, which is then dehydrated to urea, CO(NH2)2.

questions.question: A heterogeneous catalyst used in industrial processes such as the Haber and Contact processes offers the practical advantage of:
options: Being consumed and needing constant replacement
Being in a different phase from the reactants, allowing easy separation and reuse
Dissolving completely in the reaction mixture
Requiring no support or promoter materials ever
questions.correct_answer: Being in a different phase from the reactants, allowing easy separation and reuse
questions.explanation: Heterogeneous (usually solid) catalysts remain physically separate from gaseous or liquid reactants, simplifying continuous industrial processing and catalyst recovery.

questions.question: Catalyst poisoning in industrial processes refers to:
options: Deliberate addition of a promoter to boost catalytic activity
Loss of catalytic activity due to strong adsorption of impurities (e.g. sulfur compounds) onto active sites
The natural decay of radioactive catalysts
Cooling of the catalyst bed below operating temperature
questions.correct_answer: Loss of catalytic activity due to strong adsorption of impurities (e.g. sulfur compounds) onto active sites
questions.explanation: Poisons such as sulfur or arsenic compounds strongly and often irreversibly bind to active catalytic sites, blocking them and reducing or destroying catalytic activity.

questions.question: In a distillation column used as a unit operation in industry, trays or packing are included mainly to:
options: Increase the surface area for vapour-liquid contact, improving separation efficiency
Heat the feed directly
Serve only as structural support with no separation function
Condense all vapour instantly at the base
questions.correct_answer: Increase the surface area for vapour-liquid contact, improving separation efficiency
questions.explanation: Trays/packing promote repeated vapour-liquid equilibration stages along the column height, improving component separation compared with a simple single-stage still.

questions.question: Filtration as an industrial unit operation is used primarily to:
options: Separate a solid from a liquid or gas by passing the mixture through a porous medium
Increase the temperature of a liquid
Convert a gas into a liquid
Separate two miscible liquids
questions.correct_answer: Separate a solid from a liquid or gas by passing the mixture through a porous medium
questions.explanation: Filtration relies on a porous barrier (filter medium) that retains suspended solid particles while allowing the fluid phase to pass through.

questions.question: Fractional crystallisation as an industrial separation technique exploits differences in:
options: Solubility of different solutes at a given temperature
Boiling point only
Electrical charge of the compounds
Molecular colour
questions.correct_answer: Solubility of different solutes at a given temperature
questions.explanation: By controlling temperature and concentration, the least soluble component crystallises out first, allowing separation of solutes with different solubility-temperature behaviour.

questions.question: Coagulation and flocculation in industrial water treatment are used mainly to:
options: Kill pathogenic microorganisms directly
Aggregate fine suspended particles into larger flocs that settle out more readily
Remove dissolved gases from water
Adjust the pH of the water permanently
questions.correct_answer: Aggregate fine suspended particles into larger flocs that settle out more readily
questions.explanation: Coagulants (e.g. alum) neutralise the charge on colloidal particles, allowing them to clump (flocculate) into larger aggregates that can be removed by sedimentation and filtration.

questions.question: Chlorination is commonly used as a final step in municipal water treatment primarily to:
options: Disinfect the water by killing or inactivating pathogenic microorganisms
Remove all dissolved salts
Increase water hardness
Reduce the dissolved oxygen content
questions.correct_answer: Disinfect the water by killing or inactivating pathogenic microorganisms
questions.explanation: Chlorine and its active species (HOCl/OCl-) oxidise and disrupt microbial cell components, providing effective, residual disinfection of treated water.

questions.question: Effluent from an industrial plant with a high biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) is a concern mainly because, if discharged untreated, it:
options: Increases dissolved oxygen levels in receiving water bodies
Depletes dissolved oxygen in receiving water bodies as microorganisms decompose the organic matter, harming aquatic life
Has no environmental effect
Immediately neutralises water pH
questions.correct_answer: Depletes dissolved oxygen in receiving water bodies as microorganisms decompose the organic matter, harming aquatic life
questions.explanation: High-BOD effluent supports intense microbial decomposition that consumes dissolved oxygen, potentially causing hypoxia and harming fish and other aquatic organisms.

questions.question: Corrosion of iron structures in an industrial plant is fundamentally an example of which type of process?
options: A purely physical change with no chemical reaction
An electrochemical oxidation of the metal, typically forming hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust)
A nuclear decay process
A purely thermal decomposition
questions.correct_answer: An electrochemical oxidation of the metal, typically forming hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust)
questions.explanation: Rusting involves anodic oxidation of Fe to Fe2+ and cathodic reduction of oxygen (in the presence of water/electrolyte), with the resulting Fe2+ further oxidised to hydrated Fe2O3.

questions.question: Cathodic protection is used industrially to prevent corrosion of steel structures such as pipelines mainly by:
options: Coating the structure with a decorative paint only
Connecting the structure to a more reactive (sacrificial) metal, such as zinc or magnesium, which corrodes preferentially
Heating the structure continuously
Increasing the oxygen concentration around the structure
questions.correct_answer: Connecting the structure to a more reactive (sacrificial) metal, such as zinc or magnesium, which corrodes preferentially
questions.explanation: The sacrificial anode, being more easily oxidised than iron, supplies electrons to the protected structure, keeping it cathodic and suppressing its own oxidation (corrosion).

questions.question: Scrubbing of flue gases with an alkaline slurry (e.g. limestone) in industrial plants is primarily aimed at reducing emissions of:
options: Carbon dioxide only
Sulfur dioxide, which contributes to acid rain
Water vapour
Nitrogen gas
questions.correct_answer: Sulfur dioxide, which contributes to acid rain
questions.explanation: Flue-gas desulfurisation reacts SO2 with an alkaline sorbent (e.g. CaCO3/Ca(OH)2) to form calcium sulfite/sulfate, preventing SO2 release and subsequent acid rain formation.

questions.question: Industrial fermentation, such as in the production of ethanol from molasses, relies on which type of process?
options: Purely inorganic catalytic oxidation
Biological conversion of sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide by microorganisms (e.g. yeast) under anaerobic conditions
High-temperature cracking of hydrocarbons
Electrolysis of aqueous sugar solutions
questions.correct_answer: Biological conversion of sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide by microorganisms (e.g. yeast) under anaerobic conditions
questions.explanation: Fermentation uses enzymes from microorganisms like Saccharomyces cerevisiae to anaerobically convert sugars into ethanol and CO2, a key process in industrial ethanol and brewing industries.
